comparator.name: Law
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 Study Guide verifies twelve 5 EC courses in year one, eleven 5 EC requirements and one 5 EC law-and-technology choice in year two. The current regulations allocate 150 EC to required and restricted study and 30 EC to open study, with 15 EC expressly limited to the 2024–2025 and earlier cohorts. The Faculty Council’s settled sequence places the new 30 EC choice space in semester five. This record therefore lists 150 EC: 120 EC of named study and the 30 EC choice space. The revised remaining 30 EC and final-assessment allocation are unresolved. Moot court, clinic and research appear as proposed culminating formats in design material, without adopted credits or assessment rules. They are not encoded as verified requirements.
components: Methods and Techniques of Legal Research
Introduces doctrinal and empirical legal research.
This illustration selects one of three 5 EC options in law and technology.
The revised curriculum reserves 30 EC for open study, normally in semester five.

audience.programmeDescription: Leiden’s Law bachelor studies Dutch, European and international law. Students learn to interpret legislation and judgments, build legal arguments and conduct legal research.
audience.comparisonExplanation: This academic-core comparison covers the confirmed first two years of Leiden's revised Law curriculum and identifies its genuine 30-EC open study space. The final 30 EC of required study and culminating assessment are unknown and are not compared. UCR does not reproduce Leiden's full Dutch legal and procedural training; no equivalence of culminating research or professional training is established.

curriculum.limitation: The nominal degree is 180 EC. For the revised cohort, the final required 30 EC and culminating training are unconfirmed. The outgoing third year and its thesis do not apply; unknown required study is separate from the genuine 30-EC open semester.

componentNotes.law-21111004y: Introduces legal concepts, case analysis and the use of legislation and judgments. The first year also requires separate zero-credit tutoring and legal-language activities; these do not add credits to the courses shown.
componentNotes.law-21111026y: Introduces doctrinal interpretation, empirical legal research and practical research skills, building on Foundations of the Law.
componentNotes.law-22112002y: Builds on Introduction to Administrative Law and studies public decisions, enforcement, remedies and relations between government and citizens.
componentNotes.law-22112004y: Develops contract formation, interpretation, performance and termination. Entry requires Introduction to Private Law I or its former 10 EC equivalent.
componentNotes.law-22112006y: Develops substantive criminal liability after Introduction to Criminal Law.
componentNotes.law-22112008y: Develops EU internal-market law after Introduction to European Law.
componentNotes.law-22112010y: Develops liability, remedies and intellectual property. Entry requires Introduction to Private Law I or its former 10 EC equivalent; the course builds on the private-law and obligations sequence.
componentNotes.law-22112012y: Applies criminal-law principles to categories of offences, building on Introduction to Criminal Law and Substantive Criminal Law I.
componentNotes.law-22112014y: Uses economic reasoning to examine how private-law rules affect behaviour and welfare.
componentNotes.law-22112016y: Develops acquisition, loss, enforcement and security rights in property. The revised-curriculum entry requirement is completion of both introductory private-law courses.
componentNotes.law-22112020y: Develops constitutional law after Principles of Constitutional Law, including the influence of European and international law.
componentNotes.law-22112022y: Studies the formation, organisation, governance and liability of businesses. Understanding requires prior foundations in obligations and property law.
componentNotes.law-22112070y: This illustration selects Philosophy of Technology and Law. The other 5 EC choices are Entrepreneurship and Technology, and Technology and Private Law. Only one of the three counts in this slot.
componentNotes.law-y3-elective-space: The revised curriculum provides 30 EC of open study, normally in semester five. Approval is required subject to the exemptions for recognised minors and Leiden course packages. Courses must be of sufficient level and must not overlap compulsory study; Honours courses cannot count. Economics and Business Studies minors are restricted where they overlap the compulsory curriculum. Admission and places remain subject to the relevant rules.

core: Economic and business conditions of legal decisions

trace: directly Introduces public and private law, legal traditions and legal reasoning through cases.

makes a specific complementary contribution: Business planning, finance, operations and risk assessment develop the commercial decisions and transactions analysed in Transnational Business Law, for which this is an actual formal prerequisite. This is commercial-context preparation, not Dutch company-law doctrine.

makes a specific complementary contribution: Empirical research design and analysis, a complement to doctrinal work.

directly Comparative public law, constitutional institutions, judicial review and administrative remedies.

makes a specific complementary contribution: Social institutions, inequality and sociological reasoning for social context.
directly Rights instruments, institutions, cases and philosophical foundations.

alternatives.label: Law, rights and public institutions
alternatives.concept: Study legal reasoning across public, private, criminal, European, international and human-rights law. Political, social, economic and normative inquiry supports analysis of rights, institutions and disputes, with empirical research and persuasive argument. This broader legal programme does not reproduce Leiden's full Dutch doctrinal, procedural or culminating training.
alternatives.labelReason: Names the completed curricular composition and the explicitly limited academic claim.
progression: Actual workbook offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked for all six fixed terms. Advisory progression considered; no extra hard prerequisites inferred.

selection.assessment: The strongest broad legal response already sustains rights,institutions and comparative doctrine. A private/commercial-practice alternative would require further sustained private-law/procedural teaching beyond the available common palette; generic business courses and relabelled social context do not provide it. A rights-focused reordering would duplicate the closest core. The next candidate fails substantive feasibility; stop at one.

blocks: Legal traditions, case briefing, IRAC and public/private-law foundations address the introductory legal inquiry; Leiden's Dutch-law sequence is more detailed.
Sources, treaty law, state responsibility and international institutions correspond directly; national framing and scope differ.
Comparative constitutional structures, rights, judicial review and administrative foundations address identifiable public-law content; Dutch constitutional doctrine is not reproduced.
Comparative contract formation, interpretation, performance and remedies address the obligations strand; Leiden's full Dutch private-law progression differs.
The philosophical justification of rights, natural law, positivism and universality addresses a defined part of legal philosophy; human-rights focus does not reproduce all external jurisprudence.

Cross-border transactions, intellectual property, contractual remedies and legal advisory work address identifiable commercial/private-law elements; the broad Dutch liability and remedies unit is not equated.
Criminal liability, mental elements, defences and punishment address substantive criminal-law reasoning; this does not reproduce the full Dutch criminal/procedural sequence.
EU institutions, legal effect, remedies and free-movement reasoning directly overlap; the external progression and national applications differ.
Ethical analysis of AI, fairness, privacy and responsibility addresses technology's normative questions. UCR does not establish the whole law-and-technology syllabus or specific legal doctrine.
